W C H A P T E R 0 1 01 The Power of 1% Life rewards the person who shows up. This chapter explains why the smallest possible step is the smartest place to start. Progress, not perfection — one tiny step at a time. T H E 1 % R U L E e admire the dramatic transformations in movies — the training montage, the big speech, the sudden turnaround. But day-to-day life rewards something much less cinematic: the person who shows up. The 1% Rule is not about grand gestures; it’s about micro-actions. It is the art of making the smallest possible improvement you can imagine — then repeating it habitually. One push-up. Five minutes of learning. One extra glass of water. None of these will change your life today. All of them, repeated, will change your life this year. T H E Q U E S T I O N Why 1%? Because tiny changes remove friction. Friction is everything that stands between you and starting: the effort to change clothes for the gym, the mental weight of a 300-page textbook, the discomfort of a difficult conversation. The bigger the task, the more friction it carries — and the more likely you are to postpone it. 11

Shrink the task, and the friction almost disappears. You are far more likely to start the smallest of actions: one push-up, five minutes of learning, one extra glass of water. And starting is the whole game. Once you start, you often do more than you planned. Even when you don’t, you’ve kept the promise — and each small success lights up the reward centres in the brain and creates momentum. ● R E A L - W O R L D E X A M P L E The aggregation of marginal gains When Sir Dave Brailsford became performance director of British Cycling in 2003, British riders had won very little on the world stage. His strategy was deceptively simple: break everything that affects performance into tiny parts, and improve each one by about one percent. The team tested bike fit and aerodynamics, but also things no one else bothered with — which pillow helped riders sleep best (and taking it to every hotel), how to wash hands to avoid catching colds, heated shorts to keep muscles warm between races, even painting the inside of the team truck white so tiny particles of dust that could affect the bikes were easy to spot. Brailsford’s later years with Team Sky drew scrutiny on other matters, but the “marginal gains” method itself has since been adopted across sport and business. N C H A P T E R 0 2 02 The Math of Compounding One percent looks like nothing on paper. Repeated for a year, it becomes almost thirty-eight times better. Numbers sometimes hide a quiet magic. C H A P T E R 2 umbers sometimes hide a quiet magic. The expression 1.01365 looks small on paper — a one, a decimal point, a tiny exponent. In practice it becomes enormous. One percent better per day becomes roughly 37 times better after a year. That’s the mathematics of compound improvement: each day’s gain is built on top of all the gains before it, so the growth doesn’t just add up — it multiplies. 1.01365 = 37.78 · 0.99365 = 0.03 One percent better every day for a year, versus one percent worse every day for a year. 17

T W O D I R E C T I O N S Compounding works both ways Conversely, small declines compound against you. A 1% worse each day — 0.99365 — shrinks your results to almost nothing. After a year you would be left with about three percent of where you started. This dual nature of compounding means the difference between small positive choices and small negative choices grows over time into a canyon of results. On any single day, the two paths look identical. Skipping one workout doesn’t make you unfit. Eating one salad doesn’t make you healthy. Spending an hour scrolling doesn’t ruin your career. The gap is invisible on day one and enormous by day three hundred and sixty-five. E C H A P T E R 1 1 11 The Science of Small Wins Why your brain is wired to keep going once it sees progress — and how to use that wiring on purpose. Momentum is more powerful than motivation. T H E R E S E A R C H The progress principle ● R E A L - W O R L D E X A M P L E 12,000 diary entries Harvard Business School professor Teresa Amabile and psychologist Steven Kramer asked 238 people working on creative projects across seven companies to fill in a short diary at the end of every working day. Over several months they collected nearly 12,000 entries describing how people felt and what had happened. When they analysed the data, one factor stood out above all others in boosting people’s mood, motivation and creativity: making progress in meaningful work — even small progress. They called it “the progress principle” and published the findings in their 2011 book of the same name. The surprising part wasn’t that progress felt good. It was how small the progress could be and still have a large effect. A single solved problem, a small step forward, a minor breakthrough — these were often enough to turn an ordinary day into a good one. T H E B R A I N What happens inside your head When you make progress, even tiny progress, your brain’s reward system responds. A key messenger in that system is dopamine — a chemical often called the “feel-good” molecule, but better described as the “keep going” molecule. Dopamine is closely tied to motivation and learning: it helps the brain notice which actions lead to rewards, and it nudges you to repeat them. Neuroscientists have found that dopamine signals respond not just to rewards themselves but to signs that a reward is coming — cues that you’re on the right track. That’s why a ticked box, a growing streak or T H E 1 % R U L E 78
